titleEn: The LORD reigns; let the earth rejoice
progression: | C G | Am Em | F G | C C |
intro: Twelve verses, said on Friday evening as the third of the six psalms that open Kabbalat Shabbat, and verse 11 is the line recited before Kol Nidrei on the eve of Yom Kippur in Ashkenazi practice. It is a theophany: a storm arrives, the world reacts, and only afterwards is anybody told what to do about it. For a learner this is the cleanest page in the book for the third person masculine possessive in both of its shapes. Singular nouns take -o: His throne, His righteousness, His glory, His holiness. Plural nouns take -av: around Him, before Him, His foes, His lightnings, His faithful ones. Same word, his, spelled and pronounced differently depending on what it hangs from.

stichs.en: The LORD reigns; let the earth rejoice;
let the many coastlands be glad.

verses.summary: Two words carry the whole thesis and everything after them is the world reacting. The coastlands are the far edge of the map, so the claim is not a local one.

stichs.en: Cloud and thick darkness surround Him;
righteousness and justice are the foundation of His throne.

verses.summary: The throne is described from the outside inward: first what you cannot see through, then what holds the whole thing up.

stichs.en: A fire goes before Him,
and it burns up His foes all around.

verses.summary: Fire is cast as a herald rather than a weapon here, though it does the work of one on its way through.

stichs.en: His lightnings lit up the world;
the earth saw, and writhed.

verses.summary: Lightning gives one moment of complete visibility, and what the earth does with the sight is shake. Seeing here is not reassurance.

stichs.en: Mountains melted like wax before the LORD,
before the Lord of all the earth.

verses.summary: The most solid thing available is picked for the comparison, and it behaves like a candle. The second line widens the title from the name to the whole earth.

stichs.en: The heavens declared His righteousness,
and all the peoples saw His glory.

verses.summary: Two witnesses to the same event, one above and one below. The peoples get the sight without being given the interpretation.

stichs.en: Let all who serve a carved image be ashamed,
those who boast in worthless idols;
bow down to Him, all you gods.

verses.summary: What the idol worshippers get is shame rather than destruction. The last line steps past them and addresses the gods themselves.

stichs.en: Zion heard and was glad,
and the daughters of Judah rejoiced,
because of Your judgments, O LORD.

verses.summary: Zion hears where the peoples saw, and it is the judgments rather than the fire that produce the joy. This is also where the psalm first says You.

stichs.en: For You, LORD, are Most High over all the earth;
You are exalted far above all gods.

verses.summary: The reason clause. The comparison is not with other nations but with other gods, and it is made twice, both times as height.

stichs.en: You who love the LORD, hate evil;
He guards the lives of His faithful ones,
He rescues them from the hand of the wicked.

verses.summary: The psalm turns and speaks to people for the first time. It asks for something from the affections, then states twice what God does for those who manage it.

stichs.en: Light is sown for the righteous,
and gladness for the upright in heart.

verses.summary: An agricultural image and not a gift: something is in the ground and is not visible yet. This is the line said before Kol Nidrei.

stichs.en: Rejoice in the LORD, you righteous,
and give thanks to His holy name.

verses.summary: It closes with the imperative it opened with, now aimed at a named group instead of at the earth and the islands.

pardes.body: Verse 1 is the claim, verses 2 to 6 the theophany, verse 7 its effect on the idol worshippers, verse 8 its effect on Zion, verse 9 the reason, verses 10 to 12 the instruction. Watch the direction of travel: the psalm starts at the coastlands, the furthest thing it can name, and finishes on the single righteous person of {{11.2}}. Watch also what Zion is given. The peoples in verse 6, {{6.3}}, saw the glory. Zion, {{8.0}}, only heard, and it is Zion that rejoices. Hearing the report is treated as enough, which is the position the reader of the psalm is in as well.

{{1.1}} is a perfect verb and its tense is disputed. Read as a standing state it means the LORD reigns, something always true; read as an event it means the LORD has become king, an accession being announced. Liturgical use has taken it both ways, and the difference is the difference between a statement and a coronation. {{2.1}} is the word for the thick darkness at Sinai, and Deuteronomy 4:11 pairs it with cloud in the same order it appears here, so the weather in this psalm is not generic. In verse 7 the plural {{7.9}} is left unresolved: gods, angels, or powers, and translators have chosen all three.

{{11.0}} is sown, not handed over. The word {{11.1}} is a passive participle, so the light is in the ground now and the harvest is later, which is exactly why the verse can be said by people who cannot see any light at the moment. A long-standing reading connects this light to the light of the first day of creation, stored away for the righteous rather than spent. In Ashkenazi practice the line is recited before Kol Nidrei on the eve of Yom Kippur: the community states that the light exists before it says anything at all about its own failures.

The six psalms that open Kabbalat Shabbat are commonly counted against the six days of the week, and this is the third of them. Read that way the sequence is not a set of praises but a passage, each weekday handed over in turn until the week is finished and Shabbat can be received. Inside the psalm, the two halves of verse 2 give the standard mystical picture of concealment and structure held together: cloud and thick darkness are what surrounds, righteousness and justice are what the throne stands on. Nobody is asked to see through the cloud. The instruction of {{10.2}} and the exaltation of {{9.8}} both assume the base is sound without requiring it to be visible.
